title: HDFC Bank Shares Slide 5% as Margin Squeeze Overshadows Steady Q1 Profit Growth
excerpt: India's largest private lender lost nearly Rs 70,000 crore in market value after reporting a sharper-than-expected decline in net interest margins, even as brokerages maintained bullish targets.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • HDFC Bank shares fell over 5%, losing nearly Rs 70,000 crore in market value.
  • Net profit rose 5% to Rs 19,060 crore, but net interest margin contracted to 3.26%.
  • Gross advances increased 15.4% to Rs 30.6 lakh crore, driven by retail and corporate lending.
  • Brokerages maintained Buy ratings, with targets suggesting up to 28% upside from current levels.

HDFC Bank Q1 FY27 Results
  • HDFC Bank shares fell over 5% on Monday to an intraday low of Rs 774.55, erasing nearly Rs 70,000 crore in market capitalisation after Q1 FY27 results disappointed on margins.
  • Net profit rose 5% year-on-year to Rs 19,060 crore, broadly meeting estimates, but net interest margin contracted 12 basis points sequentially to 3.26%.
  • Gross advances grew 15.4% YoY to Rs 30.6 lakh crore, driven by retail and corporate lending, while provisions fell 78% year-on-year.
  • Major brokerages including Jefferies, Nomura, and Motilal Oswal retained Buy ratings, with targets implying up to 28% upside from current levels.

HDFC Bank shares tumbled more than 5% on Monday morning, hitting an intraday low of Rs 774.55 on the NSE and dragging the broader market lower, after the private lender's June-quarter earnings revealed a sharper-than-expected contraction in profit margins.

The selloff wiped out nearly Rs 70,000 crore from HDFC Bank's market capitalisation, pushing it below Rs 11.93 lakh crore. The stock's decline weighed heavily on both the Nifty 50, which fell 0.6% to 24,185.80, and the Sensex, which shed 0.72% to 77,587.23 in early trade, according to Reuters.

The Numbers Behind the Slide

HDFC Bank on Saturday reported a standalone net profit of Rs 19,060 crore for the April-June quarter of FY27, a 5% increase from Rs 18,150 crore a year earlier. The figure broadly met analyst estimates compiled by LSEG, which had pegged earnings at Rs 19,190 crore.

Net interest income — the gap between interest earned and interest paid — rose 6.7% year-on-year to Rs 33,534 crore but fell short of the market consensus estimate of Rs 34,353 crore, according to a CNBC-TV18 poll. The miss was driven by net interest margin compressing 12 basis points quarter-on-quarter to 3.26%, a level that remains well below the 4% seen before the bank's $40 billion merger with parent HDFC Ltd in 2023.

Loan growth painted a more encouraging picture. Gross advances rose 15.4% year-on-year to Rs 30.6 lakh crore at end-June, led by a pickup in retail and corporate lending. Total deposits climbed 13.3%, while provisions and contingencies plunged 78% to Rs 3,060 crore, providing some cushion to the bottom line.

Governance Overhang Persists

The results landed against a backdrop of lingering governance concerns. Former part-time chairman Atanu Chakraborty resigned in March citing "certain happenings and practices within the bank" that were not in line with his personal values. The bank has since completed a legal review that found no evidence to support those concerns, according to Reuters.

HDFC Bank appointed former bureaucrat Rajiv Kumar as chairman last month but is yet to apply for reappointment of CEO Sashidhar Jagdishan, adding a layer of leadership uncertainty that some analysts flagged as a near-term risk.

"We see some uncertainty around the RBI extending the tenure of the current CEO, given the recent developments at the bank."

Brokerage Targets Post Q1 FY27

Despite the sharp selloff, virtually every major brokerage retained its Buy rating on HDFC Bank, pointing to attractive valuations after the stock's 17% decline so far in 2026.

Jefferies kept its target at Rs 1,050, implying 28% upside, calling the bank one of its top picks and noting that the slight NII miss was offset by lower operating expenses and credit costs. Nomura set a target of Rs 950 (16% upside), raising its FY27 loan and deposit growth estimates to 16% and 17% respectively, while flagging the bank's FCNR(B) deposit scheme as a key growth lever.

Motilal Oswal reiterated its Rs 2,050 target — the most bullish on the street — arguing that margin compression was temporary and that the SME and corporate lending segments would continue to drive business growth. JM Financial, more cautious, maintained an Add rating with a Rs 900 target, noting that a liquidity coverage ratio of 115% and credit-deposit ratio of around 96% constrained the bank's ability to accelerate lending.

What the Post-Merger Journey Means for NRI Investors

For India's diaspora investors, HDFC Bank remains one of the most widely held Indian stocks in overseas portfolios. The post-merger integration — now three years in — continues to be the central investment thesis. The bank's NIM trajectory is the key metric to watch: any sustained recovery toward pre-merger levels would signal that the funding-cost gap with rivals like ICICI Bank is narrowing.

Nomura also highlighted the FCNR(B) scheme, under which the bank expects to capture significant market share in foreign-currency non-resident deposits, a product directly relevant to NRI savers seeking competitive returns on dollar holdings parked in Indian banks.

What Comes Next

The immediate focus shifts to whether HDFC Bank can demonstrate NIM improvement in coming quarters as high-cost borrowings inherited from the merger gradually roll off. Analysts across the board expect profit before tax to grow at a 15% compound rate through FY29, with return on equity settling around 13% in FY27.

At 1.8 times FY27 adjusted price-to-book and 14 times earnings — a discount to its historical trading range — the valuation argument is straightforward. The question is whether margin recovery and leadership clarity arrive fast enough to justify the patience the street is recommending.
